newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Chevron Nigeria wants review of MOUs.
newsitem.headline: Chevron Nigeria wants review of MOUs.

text.p: The chief executive of Chevron Nigeria, George Kirkland has called for a review of the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed between Nigeria and the six multinational oil firms governing their operations in the country, the national news agency reported on Friday.

Making the call in a presentation to Nigeria's Vision 2010 committee, Kirkland said rather than act as an impetus for oil companies to attain profits, the MOUs had become beneficial only to government.
Kirkland's presentation focused on making the upstream sector of the country's oil industry viable for economic development and growth by 2010.

Vision 2010 is a committee launched in October by military ruler General Sani Abacha to fashion economic policies that will bring real growth to Nigeria's gross domestic product in the same manner as in Asian nations, notably Malaysia.
Under the current MOUs oil companies are guaranteed a profit margin of $2 on each barrel of oil they produce.
"Government has been enjoying high margins because of low operational cost environment and the edge it has over profit-sharing," Kirkland said.
He said the government's inconsistency in paying joint venture cash-calls was fast becoming a constraint to increasing crude oil reserves and production.
Cash calls are payments for any joint projects between state-run oil company NNPC and the multinationals.
In the fiscal budget announced in January, government voted $2.05 billion, a 40 percent cut in the $3.32 billion budget jointly presented by the multinationals.
Apart from Chevron, the other multinationals are Royal Dutch Shell, Mobil Nigeria, Texaco, Elf Nigeria and Agip.
Chevron pumps around 401,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil in Nigeria, out of the country's total output of two million bpd.
